# Eliciting Reasoning {#sec-eliciting-reasoning}

A base model already holds far more reasoning ability than greedy decoding
reveals, and you can draw it out at inference time without touching a single
weight. This chapter is about that elicitation: the prompting and decoding
methods that turn one forward pass into a deliberation. By the end a reader can
explain why a chain of thought helps, why sampling many chains and voting beats
sampling one, when a tree or a search is worth its cost, and why a verifier is
the quiet workhorse behind best-of-N. Teaching the weights to reason is the
sibling problem of @sec-training-to-reason; here nothing is trained.

## Problem

Ask a model a multi-step question and decode greedily, and it commits to an
answer token before it has done the work that answer depends on. The
autoregressive objective of @sec-scaling-laws spends a fixed, equal slice of
compute on every token, so a problem that needs ten steps of arithmetic gets the
same single pass as a problem that needs none. The model has the sub-skills,
since pre-training saw the additions, the lookups, and the deductions, but the
decode gives them nowhere to run. The answer position is asked to integrate
everything at once.

The problem this chapter owns is how to spend more inference compute, and spend
it in the right shape, so that latent ability surfaces, without changing the
model. Two levers exist at inference time. One is the prompt, which can ask the
model to externalize intermediate steps into tokens it can then condition on.
The other is the decoding procedure, which can sample, branch, score, and select
instead of greedily taking the top token. Every method in this chapter is a
combination of those two levers.

## Design

The core idea is to make the model write its working, then exploit that the
working is now part of the context. A chain of thought is the minimal form:
prompt the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before the final
answer, and each step becomes a token sequence the later steps attend over. This
converts a single hard prediction into a sequence of easier ones, and it gives
the model room to allocate more forward passes, one per reasoning token, to a
harder problem. Wei et al. (2022) showed that a few worked examples in the
prompt elicit this, and Kojima et al. (2022) showed that even the instruction
"Let's think step by step" elicits it zero-shot. No weights move. The ability
was latent; the prompt unlocks the decode.

Once reasoning lives in tokens, the decoding procedure becomes a design space,
sketched in @fig-eliciting-reasoning-shapes. The cleanest idea is to stop trusting a single sample. A greedy chain can take a
wrong turn early and never recover. Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) samples
many chains at non-zero temperature, then marginalizes over the reasoning paths
by taking a majority vote on the final answers. The reasoning path is treated as
a latent variable to integrate out, not an output to return:

$$
\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}\left[ a(z_i) = y \right], \quad z_i \sim p_\theta(z \mid x)
$$

where each $z_i$ is a sampled chain and $a(z_i)$ is the answer it reaches. Many
paths can reach the right answer by different routes, while wrong answers tend to
scatter, so the mode of the answer distribution is a better estimate than any one
sample. This is the highest value-per-line method in the chapter: it needs no
verifier, no extra model, only more samples and a vote.

When a problem decomposes, you can shape the chain instead of just sampling it.
Least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al. 2022) asks the model first to break a
problem into ordered subproblems and then to solve them in sequence, each
conditioned on the solved ones, which lets the model generalize to problems
harder than any single exemplar in the prompt.

The richest design treats reasoning as search over a space of partial solutions.
Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al. 2023) makes each node a coherent intermediate
thought, expands several children per node, has the model self-evaluate each as
promising or not, and explores the tree with breadth-first or depth-first search,
including lookahead and backtracking. A chain is then the degenerate tree with
one child per node and no backtracking. Pushing this further, AlphaZero-style
methods (Feng et al. 2023) run Monte Carlo Tree Search over the reasoning tree,
using value estimates to decide where to expand, so compute concentrates on
promising branches rather than spreading evenly.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-eliciting-reasoning-shapes
%%| fig-cap: "Four decoding shapes that elicit and select reasoning from a fixed model. Each spends more inference compute than greedy decoding, in a different structure."
flowchart TB
  Q[Question] --> M{Decoding shape}
  M -->|one chain| CoT[Chain of thought]
  M -->|N chains, vote| SC[Self-consistency]
  M -->|branch, evaluate, backtrack| ToT[Tree of Thoughts]
  M -->|N candidates, score, pick| BoN[Best-of-N]
  CoT --> A[Answer]
  SC --> A
  ToT --> A
  BoN --> A
```

The chain, the tree, and the value-guided search differ in the shape of the
space they explore, shown in @fig-eliciting-reasoning-structure. A chain walks
one line. A tree fans out, self-evaluates each node, and can backtrack out of a
dead end. A search adds a value estimate so compute concentrates on promising
branches instead of spreading evenly.

```{dot}

digraph G {
  rankdir=TB;
  node [shape=circle, fixedsize=true, width=0.32, label="", style=filled, fillcolor="#dddddd"];
  edge [arrowsize=0.6];

  subgraph cluster_chain {
    label="Chain";
    color="#bbbbbb";
    c0 -> c1 -> c2 -> c3;
  }

  subgraph cluster_tree {
    label="Tree, branch and backtrack";
    color="#bbbbbb";
    t0 -> t1; t0 -> t2;
    t1 -> t3; t1 -> t4;
    t2 -> t5;
    t4 [fillcolor="#f4a6a6"];
    t5 [fillcolor="#f4a6a6"];
    t3 [fillcolor="#a6d8a6"];
  }

  subgraph cluster_search {
    label="Search, value-guided";
    color="#bbbbbb";
    s0 -> s1 [penwidth=2.2]; s0 -> s2 [style=dashed, color="#999999"];
    s1 -> s3 [penwidth=2.2]; s1 -> s4 [style=dashed, color="#999999"];
    s3 -> s5 [penwidth=2.2];
    s0 [fillcolor="#a6c8f0"];
    s1 [fillcolor="#a6c8f0"];
    s3 [fillcolor="#a6c8f0"];
    s5 [fillcolor="#a6d8a6"];
  }
}
```

Self-consistency votes, but a vote only works when the answer is a discrete label
to count. Best-of-N replaces the vote with a score. Sample $N$ candidate
solutions, score each with a verifier or reward model, and return the highest.
Cobbe et al. (2021) introduced this for grade-school math: train a verifier to
judge candidate solutions, generate many, and keep the one the verifier ranks
highest. The same scorer can guide the search rather than just rank the finished
output, evaluating partial states inside a tree, which is what self-evaluation
guided beam search (Xie et al. 2023) does. The verifier is the component that
turns raw samples into a selected answer, and its quality is the ceiling on what
selection can buy. That ceiling, and how it bounds test-time scaling, is the
subject of @sec-inference-time-scaling.

A vote and a score can disagree, and @fig-eliciting-reasoning-vote-vs-score shows
when. Over the same sampled chains, a vote rewards agreement and a score rewards
correctness. When a biased model is consistently wrong, the majority answer is
also wrong, and only a verifier that checks the answer against ground truth can
rescue the minority chain that happens to be right.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-eliciting-reasoning-vote-vs-score
%%| fig-cap: "Vote versus score over the same N samples. A majority vote returns the consensus 42, which is wrong. A verifier scores each chain against ground truth and selects the minority chain that reaches 37, which is right."
flowchart LR
  Q[Question] --> C1["chain 1, says 42"]
  Q --> C2["chain 2, says 42"]
  Q --> C3["chain 3, says 42"]
  Q --> C4["chain 4, says 37"]
  C1 --> V["Vote, count answers"]
  C2 --> V
  C3 --> V
  C4 --> V
  C1 --> S["Score, verifier checks each"]
  C2 --> S
  C3 --> S
  C4 --> S
  V --> VA["picks 42, wrong"]
  S --> SA["picks 37, right"]
```

## Evolution

The lineage runs from prompt to decode to search, each step adding inference
compute in a more structured shape. Few-shot chain-of-thought prompting came
first (Wei et al. 2022), establishing that the ability was latent and a prompt
could surface it. Zero-shot CoT (Kojima et al. 2022) removed even the exemplars,
showing a single instruction sufficed and that the effect was about eliciting,
not demonstrating. Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) then changed the decode
rather than the prompt, trading a single greedy chain for many sampled chains and
a vote, and it remains the strongest simple baseline because it needs nothing but
samples.

Decomposition methods like least-to-most (Zhou et al. 2022) shaped the chain so
that hard problems became sequences of easy ones. Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al.
2023) generalized the chain to a branching search with self-evaluation and
backtracking, and AlphaZero-style tree search (Feng et al. 2023) brought a
principled value-guided expansion to that tree. In parallel, the verifier line
ran from Cobbe et al. (2021), where best-of-N reranking with a trained verifier
beat a fine-tuning baseline on math, to self-evaluation guided search (Xie et al.
2023), where the score guides the search itself rather than only ranking the
output.

The arc closes back into training. Everything here elicits, at inference, what a
fixed model already contains. The natural next move is to take the traces these
methods produce, the verified-correct chains and the high-value search paths, and
train on them so the model internalizes the behavior and needs less scaffolding
at inference. That move crosses into @sec-training-to-reason, and many of its
ingredients, sampling many completions, scoring them with a verifier, keeping the
good ones, are the same ingredients seen here, now wired into a weight update
instead of a decode.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether chain-of-thought tokens are a faithful account of the computation that
produced the answer is unsettled. The optimistic reading treats the chain as the
model's actual reasoning, which would make it both a performance lever and a
window for oversight. The skeptical reading holds that the chain can be a
post-hoc rationalization: the answer is determined by computation the tokens do
not reflect, and the model can reach the same answer when the stated reasoning is
perturbed, or state reasoning that does not drive the answer. If chains are
unfaithful, then the accuracy gain is real but the interpretability it seems to
offer is not, which matters directly for the oversight argument of
@sec-oversight-control. The evidence cuts both ways and depends on task, model,
and how faithfulness is probed, so treat a visible chain as a help to accuracy
first and a faithful trace only when tested.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The verifier you can build at the data layer decides which elicitation method you
can run. Self-consistency needs only a discrete answer to vote on, so it works
wherever answers are comparable. Best-of-N and search need a scorer, and the best
scorer is a ground-truth checker, a unit test, a numeric or symbolic equality, a
proof checker, exactly the checkable-answer condition that defines
@sec-training-to-reason. Where a sound verifier exists, search and best-of-N pay
off and their ceiling is high. Where only a learned reward model exists, the same
methods inherit its over-optimization from @sec-rlhf and a stronger search can
make the answer worse by driving harder on a flawed score. The availability of a
verifier, a property of the task and not the decoder, is what sets how far
inference-time compute can be spent profitably.
:::

## Trade-offs

Each method buys accuracy with inference compute, and the exchange rate differs.

- **Single chain versus voting.** One chain is cheapest and lowest latency but
  brittle to an early wrong turn. Self-consistency multiplies token cost by the
  sample count $N$ for a robust majority answer, with diminishing returns as $N$
  grows. It needs a discrete, comparable answer, so it does not apply to
  open-ended generation where there is nothing to vote on.
- **Voting versus scoring.** A vote needs no extra model but cannot rank
  free-form outputs and cannot tell a confidently-wrong consensus from a correct
  one. Best-of-N needs a verifier or reward model but ranks anything that scorer
  covers, and its ceiling rises with verifier quality. A vote rewards agreement; a
  score rewards correctness, and they diverge when the model is consistently
  wrong.
- **Chain versus tree versus search.** A chain spends compute in one line. A tree
  spends it on breadth and can backtrack out of dead ends, at the cost of many
  self-evaluation calls per node, which are themselves model calls that can be
  wrong. MCTS-style search concentrates compute on high-value branches but adds
  the machinery and the dependence on a value estimate that, if miscalibrated,
  steers the search wrong. The gain over self-consistency is real but smaller than
  its cost on many tasks, so the simpler method is often the right default.
- **Compute now versus training once.** Every method here pays its cost on every
  query, forever. Training the behavior in, per @sec-training-to-reason, pays once
  and amortizes, but costs a training run and the data to do it. Elicitation is
  the right tool when the model is fixed, the task is new, or the volume is low;
  internalization wins at scale.

## Implementation

The methods compose more than they compete, and the practical recipe stacks them.
Chain-of-thought is the substrate: get the model to externalize steps, by
exemplars or by a step-by-step instruction. On top of it, self-consistency is the
first upgrade, sample a handful to a few dozen chains and vote, because it is
cheap to add and needs no other component. When a verifier exists, best-of-N over
the same samples replaces the vote with a score and lifts the ceiling. A tree or
a search is the heaviest tool, justified when the problem has a real branching
structure and dead ends that backtracking escapes, and when the per-node
self-evaluation is reliable enough to trust.

The failure modes are specific. A vote over an unreliable model can be
confidently wrong, since self-consistency reports the consensus, not the truth,
and a biased model agrees with itself. A weak verifier makes best-of-N worse than
a single sample once $N$ is large, because selection pressure finds the
verifier's blind spots, the inference-time face of the reward hacking in
@sec-rlhf. A tree search with a miscalibrated self-evaluation spends its budget
exploring bad branches and pruning good ones, so the search can underperform the
plain chain it generalizes. And the cost is real on every call: a method that
multiplies token count by tens for a few points of accuracy may not survive the
economics of @sec-economics, which is why the field's center of gravity moved
toward training the behavior in.

Two structural boundaries keep elicitation honest. It cannot exceed what the
fixed model can produce, only surface and select among it, so a problem the model
never solves in any sample is out of reach no matter how many you draw or how
hard you search. And the visible chain is a lever on accuracy, not a guaranteed
account of the computation, so reading it as oversight, per
@sec-oversight-control, is a claim that needs its own test, not a free byproduct
of asking the model to think out loud.
